sources.title: Cainiao interview note preserving the 100-million package interval question
Writer deterministic and randomized interval validation

claims.text: The source asks for the peak not-yet-picked-up package time range, its duration, and time/space complexity from about 100 million same-day put/take records; it does not prescribe precision, endpoint semantics, language, or a specific algorithm.
Half-open [put,take), nonnegative integer offsets, Java, all peak segments, and total peak duration are explicit answer-side choices rather than source facts.

Under the declared half-open contract, the grouped endpoint implementation matches an independent direct-membership oracle across exhaustive small multisets, independently seeded random cases, simultaneous boundaries, disjoint peaks, and large sparse timestamps.

Sorting 2n endpoints gives O(n log n) time and O(n) event storage; a fixed small time domain permits O(n+T) time and O(T) storage. Two hundred million primitive long endpoints are about 1.6 GB decimal before JVM/input/output overhead.

validation.command: compile PackagePeak.java with javac -Xlint:all -Werror; compare to independent direct-membership boundary-span oracle over exhaustive small multisets and independently seeded randomized cases
validation.reported_stdout: PASS exhaustive_cases=15504 random_cases=5000 direct_membership_oracle=pass simultaneous_boundary=pass disjoint_peaks=pass large_sparse_time=pass invalid_contract=reject
checks: 15504 exhaustive interval multisets match direct-membership oracle
5000 independently seeded randomized interval sets match direct-membership oracle
simultaneous boundary continuity and disjoint equal peaks match declared half-open contract
large sparse timestamps near encoding limit match oracle

boundary_tests.expected: endpoint semantics, Java/API, all-peaks return shape and algorithm choice remain explicit answer-side decisions
all deltas at one timestamp are combined and occupancy is evaluated on the following positive-length span
all disjoint equal maxima are retained and adjacent uninterrupted peak spans merge
event-array estimate is approximately 1.6 GB decimal and is not represented as total process memory

findings: The primary interview note asks for the time range with the most not-yet-picked-up packages, that range duration, and time/space complexity for about 100 million same-day put/take records; it does not prescribe timestamp precision, endpoint semantics, language, Difference Array, Sweep Line, or one specific return shape.

The candidate explicitly labels half-open [put,take), nonnegative integer offsets, Java, returning all peak segments, and summing peak duration as answer-side contracts rather than recovered source facts.

The grouped-endpoint sweep invariant is correct under that contract: after all changes at t are applied, current is exactly the active-package count on [t,next), and adjacent equal-peak spans remain continuous when a boundary has net delta zero.

Reviewer-owned validation compiles the committed Java implementation with warnings as errors and compares it to an independent direct-membership oracle that counts interval containment on every distinct boundary span, not to the writer delta-sweep implementation.

The reviewer covers all 15,504 multisets of up to five intervals over a six-boundary toy domain, 5,000 independently seeded randomized cases, simultaneous put/take boundaries, disjoint equal peaks, large sparse timestamps near the declared encoding limit, and invalid inputs.

The O(n log n) general endpoint-sort bound and O(n+T)/O(T) fixed-domain alternative are correctly distinguished. Two hundred million primitive long endpoints consume about 1.6 GB in decimal units; the answer explicitly excludes JVM/input/output overhead from that estimate and separately warns that production input layout must be validated.

The illustrative List<Interval> API is not itself a memory-optimal representation for 100 million records, but the candidate does not present the 1.6 GB event array as total process memory and explicitly directs real-scale implementations toward primitive input layouts, fixed buckets, streaming/merge, or external sorting as constraints permit.
No fabricated production experience, unsupported claim that the source mandated a specific algorithm, placeholder implementation, or uncovered source variant was found.
